app.title: Cosmic Atlas
app.description: A navigable 3D map of the universe, from the Sun's neighbourhood to the cosmic web.
app.canvas: 3D map of the universe. Drag to orbit, scroll or pinch to zoom, W A S D to fly, click a point for details.

scale.label: Scale
tour.scale.label: Scale tour
tour.scale.sun.title: The Sun
tour.scale.sun.text: Home. This view is about 200 AU across; the nearest star is 270,000 times farther than the Earth is from the Sun.
tour.scale.proxima.title: Proxima Centauri
tour.scale.proxima.text: The nearest star, 1.30 pc away. Its light takes 4.2 years to reach us.
tour.scale.neighbourhood.title: The solar neighbourhood
tour.scale.neighbourhood.text: Stars within 1 kpc of the Sun, the reach of Gaia parallaxes in this map. Light crosses it in about 6,500 years.
tour.scale.milky-way.title: The Milky Way
tour.scale.milky-way.text: Our galaxy seen face-on. This is a model of the spiral arms (Reid et al. 2019), not data. The Sun sits 8.3 kpc from the centre.
tour.scale.local-group.title: The Local Group
tour.scale.local-group.text: The Milky Way, Andromeda and their satellites, about 3 Mpc across.
tour.scale.cosmic-web.title: The cosmic web
tour.scale.cosmic-web.text: Galaxies trace filaments around empty voids. Light from the far side of this view left {edgeLookback}.
rail.label: Scale, as camera distance
help.title: Controls
help.v.zoom: Zoom toward the cursor, one decade every few notches
help.k.fly: W A S D, Q E
help.v.fly: Fly; Shift is faster. Speed follows the current scale
help.v.keys: Orbit and zoom from the keyboard
help.v.click: Details of the brightest point under the cursor
credits.sesame: Name resolution: CDS Sesame (via the VizieR mirror at CfA). Distances for redshifts use Planck18 comoving distance.
credits.skymap: Rendering techniques (subtree blobs, solid-angle photometry, GPU picking, label declutter) adapted from skymap by Alexander Rulkens (MIT).
docs.fallback: This article is not available in English yet.
docs.placeholder: This article is still being written; a short outline is shown for now.
docs.missing.title: Article not found
docs.missing.text: There is no article called “{slug}” yet. The contents list shows every article.
layer.solar.meta: Live positions from astronomy-engine; probe tracks from JPL Horizons.
time.label: Simulation time
solar.note.body: Position from astronomy-engine {version} at the time shown in the time bar. Radius: IAU WGCCRE 2015 (Archinal et al. 2018). Mass and period: NASA planetary fact sheets.
solar.note.craft: Track: JPL Horizons heliocentric vectors every 30 days ({span}), cubic Hermite interpolation.
solar.note.moons_missing: Phobos and Deimos are not shown: astronomy-engine has no ephemeris for them.
solar.credit: Solar System: positions from astronomy-engine 2.1.19 (MIT, Don Cross); probe tracks from JPL Horizons; textures: Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0), Earth: NASA Blue Marble Next Generation (NASA Earth Observatory).
tour.scale.earth.title: Earth and the Moon
tour.scale.earth.text: Our planet and its Moon, 384,400 km apart on average. Light crosses that gap in 1.3 seconds.
tour.scale.mars.title: Mars
tour.scale.mars.text: Half the size of Earth. Depending on where both planets are, its light takes 3 to 22 minutes to reach us.
tour.scale.jupiter.title: Jupiter and its moons
tour.scale.jupiter.text: The largest planet, with Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto, the four moons Galileo saw in 1610.
shape.how.hips: HiPS tiles from {host}, reprojected in the browser (hips2fits unavailable)
shape.how.error: not available ({error}); the procedural disk is shown
shape.how.later: loaded when the galaxy is large on screen
shape.how.off: image loading is off (?thumbs=off), the procedural disk is shown
shape.note: Image: {survey} HiPS, {credit}; {how}. The image is the view from Earth, shown on the disk plane oriented by PA and inclination, so it is approximate when seen from far from the Sun.
showme.label: Show me
showme.title: Fly from the cosmic web down to where you are
showme.locating: Finding your location… it stays in this browser and is never sent anywhere.
showme.denied: Location not available ({msg}). The flight will stop at Earth.
tour.me.web.title: The cosmic web
tour.me.web.text: Every dot is a galaxy: 15 million of them, mapped by DESI. One of them is ours.
tour.me.lg.title: The Local Group
tour.me.lg.text: Our neighbourhood of galaxies: the Milky Way, Andromeda and dozens of dwarf galaxies, a few million light-years across.
tour.me.mw.title: The Milky Way
tour.me.mw.text: Our galaxy: 100 to 400 billion stars in a disc about 100,000 light-years wide. The Sun is about 27,000 light-years from the centre.
tour.me.near.title: The Sun and its neighbours
tour.me.near.text: The nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is 4.2 light-years away. Its light left when you were 4 years younger.
tour.me.solar.title: The Solar System
tour.me.solar.text: Eight planets around one star. Light from the Sun takes about 4 hours to reach Neptune.
tour.me.earth.title: Earth
tour.me.earth.text: A planet 12,742 km across. Sunlight takes 8 minutes 20 seconds to get here.
tour.me.region.title: Your part of the world
tour.me.region.text: Seen from 4,500 km up, at the real time of day; at night the lights are the cities, as seen by the Suomi NPP satellite.
tour.me.here.title: You are here
tour.me.here.text: Even now you are moving: Earth carries you around the Sun at about 30 km/s, and the Sun carries us around the galaxy at about 230 km/s.
bh.hud.title: Near {name}
bh.hud.clock.ratio: 1 s for you = {k} s far away
bh.hud.spaghetti: Spaghettification: your head and feet are pulled apart at {g} g
bh.hud.floor: Stopped at 1.5 r_s, the photon sphere: here light itself can circle the hole. Closer in, hovering takes ever more thrust, and at r_s, the event horizon, no thrust is enough: nothing that crosses it, not even light, comes back out. The map stops you here.
bh.hud.static: You hover in place (a static observer). Lensing is a ray-traced Schwarzschild metric; no spin.
bh.hud.webgl: Lensing is off (?bhlens=off), so the sky is not bent here. The numbers above are exact.
bh.hud.webgl2: WebGL 2 fallback: the same lens shader compiled to GLSL, at Low quality by default.
bh.disk.src.m87: Disk tilt from the M87 jet (17° to the line of sight, PA 288°; Walker et al. 2018), clockwise flow (EHT 2019).
bh.disk.src.sgra: Disk tilt from GRAVITY flare orbits (i = 155°, PA 177°; GRAVITY 2023), clockwise.
bh.disk.src.none: Disk orientation unknown; drawn in the Galactic plane.
bh.disk.note: Illustrative thin disk: Novikov–Thorne temperature profile from the ISCO (3 r_s) to {rout} r_s, peak {tpeak} K, Doppler beaming and gravitational redshift (I ∝ g⁴). The real {name} feeds through a hot, thick flow that the EHT sees in radio, not a thin optical disk.
bh.mass.approx: Catalogue mass is a range or bound; its midpoint is used.
bh.flamm.label: Flamm’s paraboloid z = 2√(r_s(r − r_s)): a diagram of curved space, not an object
time.epoch.label: Star time: shift from now, −1 Myr to +1 Myr, logarithmic
time.starsHint: Drag to move the stars along their measured space velocities, up to ±1 Myr.
time.starsNote: Straight-line motion from Gaia velocities. It ignores the Galaxy’s gravity, so beyond about 1 Myr it is a poor guide (Bailer-Jones 2015, A&A 575, A35). Stars without a measured radial velocity move only across the sky and fade. Layers without velocities, labels of nearby objects and the glow of distant star clouds stay at today’s positions.
layers.preview: {stars}; {pct} % of the sky downloaded so far; with space velocities
row.velocityTangential: {v} km/s across the sky; no radial velocity measured
row.velocityNone: no proper motion: does not move here
info.epochNote: Position moved on a straight line with the Gaia DR3 velocity; Galactic orbits are ignored.
